title: The Hypercorrection Effect
author: Bradley Busch
summary: Bradley Busch introduces the Hypercorrection Effect - the finding that people are more likely to remember a correction when they were both wrong and highly confident beforehand - and walks through the research base behind it for a teacher audience. He explains the dominant "learning surprise" theory: confident errors violate a person's existing mental model, and that violation itself triggers deeper processing of the correct information through three mechanisms - challenged overconfidence, interrupted confirmation bias, and heightened metacognitive awareness. He cites supporting evidence including a study showing higher-confidence wrong answers are corrected more durably than low-confidence ones, and fMRI research locating the effect in the brain's medial frontal area, associated with attention and surprise. Busch also frames the effect through episodic memory, arguing that being wrong creates a memorable event that anchors the later correction more firmly than a neutral piece of new information would. His classroom-facing conclusions are practical: give corrective feedback immediately after an error rather than delaying it, and build a classroom culture that treats mistakes as normal and useful rather than something to avoid, since normalizing errors is what allows students to benefit from the effect in the first place.
points: Busch names three psychological mechanisms behind the effect - overconfidence disruption, interruption of confirmation bias, and increased metacognitive awareness - all triggered by the "learning surprise" of being wrong while confident.
He cites fMRI evidence locating the effect in the medial frontal cortex, the brain region tied to attention and surprise, giving the folk phenomenon a neurological anchor.
The practical takeaway is that high-confidence errors need immediate corrective feedback, since delay weakens the episodic memory trace that makes the correction stick.

Busch frames the effect as a case for building a classroom culture where mistakes are treated as opportunities rather than failures, since the emotional charge of being wrong is part of what makes the correction memorable.
quotes: The Hypercorrection Effect suggests that when we are both wrong and confident about something, then get corrected through feedback, we are more likely to remember the right information.
The dominant explanation suggests that the Hypercorrection Effect occurs due to learning surprise, which refers to the moment when students discover that their prediction was incorrect.
The researchers discovered that participants were more likely to remember the correct answers for questions they had previously answered incorrectly with high confidence as opposed to low confidence.

When comparing brain activations in response to feedback on high- and low-confidence errors, researchers discovered neural activity in the medial frontal area, which is responsible for attention and surprise.

Research suggests that when students make learning errors and experience the Hypercorrection Effect, it creates an episodic memory, which is the memory of events. This type of memory reinforces the correction

The Hypercorrection Effect is most prominent when students receive corrective feedback immediately after an error. This allows them to quickly correct their misconceptions and reinforce the correct information in their memory.

Given that errors are inevitable in learning, the Hypercorrection Effect is one powerful, simple and effective way you can correct errors in your students’ knowledge base without diminishing their learning spirit.
